sections.body: Artificial intelligence in medicine is not a future promise. It is already reading chest X-rays and CT scans for fractures, bleeds and nodules, drafting clinical notes from recorded conversations, guiding robotic instruments during knee and spine procedures, flagging patients in intensive care whose vital signs are deteriorating, screening millions of chemical compounds for drug candidates, triaging patient messages, modeling disease spread across counties, and decoding brain signals for prosthetics and speech aids. In genomics it matches tumor mutations to possible therapies. In regulation it logs how these tools are cleared, monitored and secured. The work is narrow, task specific and unevenly distributed across hospitals and countries.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The most settled area is imaging, where many tools have regulatory clearance and are used daily, but a radiologist still signs the report. Documentation tools reduce typing yet can introduce errors that a clinician must review. Predictive analytics in intensive care can warn of sepsis or kidney injury, but false alarms remain common and the benefit over standard scoring is debated. Surgical robots assist rather than operate on their own, and drug discovery models accelerate early screening but the slow, expensive part is still human trials. This site tracks 1000 medical AI models and 805 scientific models, but a model in a registry is not proof it works in a clinic. Six active product liability and wrongful death lawsuits against AI companies are tracked here, a reminder that failures carry real consequences.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: Start with Diagnostic Imaging and Radiology for the most mature clinical use, then turn to Genomic Medicine and Precision Therapeutics for how models link variants to treatment. Clinical Documentation and Ambient Intelligence covers the daily burden of notes, while Surgical Robotics and Navigation shows machines in the operating room. Predictive Patient Analytics and Intensive Care explains early warning systems, and Drug Discovery and Molecular Simulation covers the search for new compounds. Telemedicine and Triage and Epidemiology and Population Health move from individual access to outbreak tracking. Neuroinformatics and the Brain covers brain data and brain machine interfaces, and Governance, Compliance and Medical Device Security closes with the rules, audits and security risks around all of it.
